entities.summary:
The Masnavi, authored by Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Rumi in the 13th century, is a seminal Persian poetic work that profoundly impacted Sufi thought and literature. Comprising six books, its 25,000 verses weave intricate narratives and moral parables that explore themes of divine love, spiritual yearning, and the human condition. Rumi, a mystic from the city of Balkh in present-day Afghanistan, wrote this masterpiece during a period of significant cultural and intellectual flourishing within the Islamic Golden Age, which spanned from the 8th to the 14th centuries.

The Masnavi was completed around 1273, shortly before Rumi's death, and serves not only as a poetic anthology but also as a spiritual guide for Sufis and laypersons alike. It employs a unique blend of storytelling, allegory, and philosophical discourse, drawing on various sources, including the Quran, Persian folklore, and the works of previous poets and philosophers. The text is structured in rhymed couplets, allowing for lyrical expression and accessibility, which contributed to its widespread popularity across the Persian-speaking world and beyond.

The legacy of the Masnavi endures through its translation into numerous languages and its influence on later poets, philosophers, and spiritual leaders. It has inspired various movements within Sufism and continues to be a vital part of Islamic literature and spiritual practice. The work's themes of unity, love, and the quest for God resonate across cultures, making it a timeless masterpiece that bridges the divide between the spiritual and the secular.

As Rumi famously said, 'The wound is the place where the Light enters you,' encapsulating the Masnavi's core message that suffering can lead to enlightenment and deeper understanding of the divine. Its impact on literature, spirituality, and intercultural dialogue remains significant to this day, reflecting the universal quest for meaning and connection.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Masnavi (Persian: مثنوی معنوی, Maṡnavī-ye Maʿnavī, 'Spiritual Couplets') is a six-volume poem in rhyming couplets (masnavi metre) by the Persian Sufi poet and mystic Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Rūmī (1207–1273), composed in Konya (in present-day Turkey) c. 1258–1273 at the instigation of his disciple Husam al-Din Chalabi. Running to approximately 25,000 couplets (51,000 lines) and one of the longest poems in any language, the Masnavi is the summit of Persian Sufi poetry and the work that earned Rumi the title 'Mawlana' (Our Master). It is sometimes called 'the Quran of the Persian language' — a reflection of its central position in Persian literary and spiritual culture.

The Masnavi's structure is associative rather than linear — it moves through stories, parables, Quranic commentary, philosophical discussions, and lyrical passages in a manner that enacts the Sufi understanding of spiritual reality as a web of interconnected meanings rather than a sequential argument. Its opening verses — the 'reed flute' (ney) passage — are among the most famous in all of Persian literature: the image of the reed flute's music as the cry of separation from its origin (the reed bed) as an allegory of the soul's longing for union with the divine is one of the defining metaphors of Sufi thought. The Masnavi contains dozens of embedded stories — many drawn from the Quran, Hadith, Persian folk tradition, and Hindu narratives — that are used as vehicles for Sufi teaching: the story of the reed flute, the elephant in the dark room (a parable for the divine beyond human comprehension), the three fishermen, the lion who hunts alone (on free will and divine help), and hundreds of others.

Rumi's Masnavi has been translated into dozens of languages and is among the best-selling poetry collections in the United States in the late 20th and early 21st centuries (in the translations of Coleman Barks, which, though free paraphrases, introduced millions of English-speaking readers to Sufi mystical poetry).
